segments.text: Uh, FEC, and we look forward to your submission.
We've got you for five minutes, but please leave some time for questions.
Will do.
So, the Fair Trading Amendment Bill has, in my view,
very admirable objectives. Two key objectives as
I read the explanatory note are ensuring
that the Fair Trading Act is fit for purpose
as digital markets evolve,
and secondly, enabling efficient and effective
enforcement.
And by efficient, I take that to mean
cost effective.
Effective really means timely.
In my view, unfortunately, the Fair Trading Act has become
ineffective in relation to digital markets, particularly in the
case of overseas online trades,
and hugely costly to try and enforce against overseas online traders.
In my written submission, I give the example of
Viagogo, the online ticket reseller.
And just to give a just very brief overview, Commission wanted to
stop
some conduct by Viagogo in terms of the
way that they were offering tickets for resale.
Brought a case in 2018, wanted an injunction.
Viagogo avoided service, said, "You've got to service in Switzerland,
go through The Hague convention, do it through diplomatic channels."
Argued in the meantime that the High Court didn't have jurisdiction to grant an
injunction, actually won that in the High Court.
Court of Appeal had to take that on appeal to the Court of Appeal.
Viagogo took all steps to try and resist the
proceedings, resisted discovery, sought to delay the
proceedings. The Commission said that they took an obstructive attitude.
I
don't know the rights and wrongs of that, but certainly the High Court made some
critical comments.
Continued their defense,
despite being penalized for essentially the same conduct in Australia in
2020. So the case took six years, from
2018 to 2024, and then
since then it's gone further on appeal.
And cases like that are hugely expensive and time-consuming,
very hard for the Commerce Commission to run more than one or two cases like
that at the same time if they
involve that much expense. And in the meantime, you've got ongoing harm to
consumers over many years
if online traders can't be quickly prevented
from engaging in misleading conduct.
Now fortunately,
we've got a good model in other legislation for how to deal with this.
So the Financial Markets Conduct Act provides a
model in relation to how to deal with misleading conduct in financial markets.
So the FMA is the regulator for misleading conduct in financial markets,
Commerce Commission for everything else, misleading conduct in other markets.
And what you can do under the Financial Markets Conduct Act
is the regulator can give notice of a stop order,
so the trader has to stop the misleading conduct immediately.
They can challenge
that order in the courts, but at least the consumer harm is prevented in the
meantime. And if the trader doesn't stop the conduct, then the
regulator can, as part of the stop order notice,
stop the trader from providing services in New Zealand
to New Zealand consumers at all. The Financial
Markets Authority has exercised its stop order power
to prevent a Dubai corporation from offering securities when the
public was misled. I refer to that case, that example, in
my written submission.
And so that enabled the FMA, in that case, within two months
of finding out about the misleading conduct, to stop securities
being offered.
So
my essential argument is that the Commerce Commission should have the same
power to
give stop notices as
the FMA has.
Same sort of situation to stop misleading conduct.
And in my view, that's a far more important reform than just
increasing the penalties under the act.
Now, I don't have a problem with what's currently proposed in
the Amendment Bill. I'm just saying that if you really want to achieve the
objectives of the
Bill, of ensuring effective and efficient
enforcement of the act, and if you really want to achieve the
objective in the Bill of ensuring that
the Fair Trading Act is fit for purpose as digital markets
evolve, then you need these stop order powers more than you need the
increased penalties, though I don't mind the increased penalties.
Thanks, John. Thanks. Quick question from me.
The stop order power,
you're saying FMA already has it.
If the Commerce Commission have it, are you saying it would...
I'm just making sure we're not duplicating powers.
Would it be a separate type for different entities?
Yeah. So both the Commerce Commission would have as well as the FMA.
The FMA, of course, only regulate misleading conduct in
relation to financial markets,
whereas the Commerce Commission regulates misleading conduct everywhere else.
Okay.
So it's to try and have consistency and ensure that the
Commission has the same toolbox.
Yeah. Thank you. Your submission's very clear and very comprehensive-
Mm
... for a person's submission, so I just want to thank you for that, and that'll be
duly noted.
Very good. Any other questions from the committee?
Unfortunately, we have met time, but-
Okay
... yeah.
No worries.

Thank you.

we're responsible for administering and maintaining the .nz
domain name system, the DNS-

registry and the infrastructure that enables .nz
websites and email addresses to connect
globally.

system,

whole
sub- the whole area that you're considering.

specific feedback in relationship to this bill.
Thanks, Isabel.
Thank you. I'm going to introduce

understand the nature of the tools that we have
because we have got a request for a-

.nz registry, actually has the

offending content or take
down...

top-level domain name sys- um, operators, like
InternetNZ, who runs the top
of .nz. So they have the full

We're saying that it's much more effective if a registry
is also
able to have the benefits of the safe harbor, and at the
moment,
it's not clear that we're included.
So I'm not going to read out the whole basis
of our written submission, but we have proposed wording
there. We say that the policy intent is better
achieved if it's clarified that both
the wholesalers and retailers of
domain names are covered by the safe harbor.
And we are in an environment where
organizations like the Domain Name Commission and other threat
providers are also doing
scam prevention. So we want to extend- The definition
of registration services to those providing
oversight and compliance services.
So I hope
that nuance can be adapted and that will
better provide for the intent of the legislation, the
policy intent, so that all of the key parties can
actually obtain that safe harbor. Thank you.
Thank you. We've got a question from Todd Stevens.
Oh, no, mine was just a comment to say thanks for your submission.
Yeah, we'll definitely take that on board.
And you've outlined your case pretty clearly, so thank
you.
So just the other key point we wanted to make
relates to the trusted flagger network set out the accompanying
regulatory impact statement as a non-legislative
option that's currently being scoped.
We recommend the trusted flagger network could be given greater
status and legislated.
Giving the trusted flagger network a statutory mandate would provide
entities acting in scam disruption, including the Domain Name
Commission, the assurance that the actions are proportionate and
meet the legal threshold for safe harbor.
So I think that was the second key point we wanted to bring to your attention.
Very good. Okay. Thank you very much for your presentation, Vivian and Isabel.
We have met time, but, appreciate that.
We'll feed into our select committee process.
Okay. Thank you.
Thank you.

I'm not fully against this bill or
anything.
I agree with stopping big multinationals from
treating fines as a cost of doing business,
giving the Commerce Commission a faster enforcement tool,
fighting online scams and updating product
safety standards faster.
But I have a few worries.
I'm worried about the overwhelming volume of legislation
being rushed through Parliament.
When laws move at this pace, frequently
strip back treaty protections, it creates
deep anxiety across our community.
Compared to major constitutional changes, a consumer
bill might not look like the primary concern, but when
Parliament moves in haste, officials neglect
critical mechanisms buried in the fine print.
So why would citizens not scrutinize
every detail?
Under the banner of consumer protection, this bill shifts
enforcement
from a criminal regime requiring proof beyond
reasonable doubt with $600,000
fine caps to a civil regime with a lower
balance of probabilities standard
and penalties up to $5 million. This
expansion comes right off the back of
a recent public sector budget cut to the Commerce
Commission. Will
the Commission actually have the resources needed to manage this massive
increase in litigation capacity, or
will enforcement simply fail to
private
competitors filing costly civil lawsuits?
In primary industries like farming and fishing, minor
operational slips like an uncalibrated
scale on a boat or a packing typo on
produce become easy targets. As the Insurance
Council of New Zealand highlighted, standard
statutory liability insurance does not cover
civil pecuniary penalties. While
multinationals absorb civil
litigation out of global reserves,
local Kiwi operators and Māori enterprises face an
uninsurable liability gap. How can we
justify exposing local operators to sudden
liquidation over an honest operational mistake?
The most severe oversight, however, is how the regime
interacts with Whenua Māori. While Section
342 of Te Tiriti Whenua Māori
Act protects land titles from direct
execution, this bill creates an
indirect economic
backdoor.
A multimillion-dollar penalty forced onto a trading arm
triggers corporate insolvency. The High Court
liquidator can seize fishing quota, livestock, and
machinery, or lease out the Whenua to third
parties to pay court debts. What is the value of
protecting land titles on paper if the commercial
engine funding Whenua housing, environmental
care, and local jobs is wiped out underneath it?
I urge the committee to- Direct officials to engage
directly with Te Puni Kōkiri to
assess these indirect commercial impacts to
include and express
savings
or
safe harbor provision protecting existing rights under Te
Ture Whenua Māori Act and Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
Tena koutou.
